about: Long-text test: pages of ordinary prose (none of the 10 filter topics) with one needle hidden inside. Needles per filter: two passing mentions (one sentence about something else that touches the topic), the filter's first direct passage, and its first look-alike (should stay quiet). The pages alone measure false alarms over a long text.
pages: The office moved to a new building in March, and it took most of the spring for everyone to settle in. The desks are arranged in long rows by the windows, and the meeting rooms are named after rivers, which confuses visitors who are told to go to the Severn or the Trent. The lifts are slow in the mornings, so a lot of people have started using the stairs, and the facilities team put up posters encouraging it. On the second floor there is a quiet room with soft chairs where people can read or make private phone calls. The printer on our side has a habit of jamming whenever someone tries to print more than twenty pages, and there is a handwritten sign above it asking people to be patient.

Every Monday the team has a planning meeting that is supposed to last half an hour and usually lasts an hour. We go through the list of tasks for the week, check who is on holiday, and agree which reports need to go out first. The manager likes to write everything on the whiteboard in three colours, and someone always takes a photo of it at the end so it can be shared in the group chat. Last week the projector stopped working halfway through, so we finished the meeting by gathering around a laptop. Afterwards there was a long discussion about whether to replace the projector or simply use the large screen in the corner.

Getting to work involves a short walk, a train and then another walk through the town centre. The train is usually on time, although on wet days it seems to slow down for no obvious reason. Most passengers read, listen to music or stare out of the window at the fields and the backs of houses. There is one conductor who announces every station in a cheerful voice and wishes everyone a pleasant day, which makes people smile even when the carriage is crowded. On the way back the platform is busier, and if the first train is full it is better to wait for the next one, which is often almost empty.

The town library reopened after a long refurbishment and now has a bright reading area, a small exhibition space and a row of computers that anyone can book for an hour. The librarians have started a monthly book group that meets on the first Tuesday, and this month they are reading a long novel about a family who run a printing business. Children's story time on Saturday mornings is so popular that they have added a second session. There are also volunteers who help older residents set up email accounts and video calls, and a noticeboard full of leaflets about evening classes in drawing, languages and local history.

At home the main project this year has been sorting out the spare room. For a long time it was full of boxes that had never been unpacked after the last move, along with a broken lamp, an exercise bike nobody used and several bags of old clothes. Over a few weekends we went through everything, gave the clothes to a charity shop, sold the bike online and kept only the things that were actually needed. The walls were repainted a pale grey, a new blind was fitted, and a desk was put under the window. It now works as a small study, and it is surprising how much calmer the whole house feels with one less cluttered room.

The internet connection has been unreliable for weeks, dropping out every evening around the same time. The provider ran several remote tests and suggested restarting the router, which helped for a day or two. Eventually an engineer came round, checked the line from the street, replaced a faulty connector in the wall and fitted a new router. Since then the connection has been steady, and video calls no longer freeze in the middle of a sentence. The engineer also explained how to move the router to a more central spot so that the signal reaches the upstairs rooms, which turned out to be a simple change that made a big difference.

My sister has taken up knitting and is making scarves for half the family. She started with simple patterns from a book borrowed from the library and has moved on to more complicated designs with cables and stripes. She says it helps her relax after work and gives her something to do with her hands while she listens to audiobooks. Her first attempts were uneven, but the latest scarf is neat and soft, and she is already planning a blanket for the winter. She has joined a small group that meets in a community hall on Wednesday evenings, where people share tips, swap wool and talk about everything except work.

The local council has announced plans to resurface several streets in our area over the summer. Letters were sent to residents explaining which roads would be closed and for how long, along with a map showing the diversions. There will be some disruption, especially for people who park on the street, but most neighbours agree that the work is overdue because the potholes have been getting worse. The council has also promised to add new pedestrian crossings near the primary school and to repaint the faded lines at the junction by the post office. A public meeting will be held in the town hall next month for anyone who wants to ask questions.

The school term ended with a concert in the main hall. Parents squeezed onto rows of plastic chairs while the children performed songs they had been practising for weeks. The youngest class sang a song about the seasons with actions for each verse, and the older pupils played a short piece on recorders and keyboards. A few of the teachers joined in for the final number, which got the loudest applause of the evening. Afterwards there was a raffle with prizes donated by local shops, and the money raised will go towards new books for the classrooms and a trip to a museum in the autumn.

Learning a new piece of software at work has taken longer than expected. The company switched to a different system for tracking projects, and everyone had to attend two training sessions. The new system has more features than the old one, but the menus are arranged differently and it is easy to lose track of where things are. A colleague has written a short guide with screenshots, which has become the most useful document on the shared drive. After a few weeks most people are comfortable with the basics, although there are still complaints about the number of notifications it sends.

The town has a small museum in an old house near the market square. It has rooms about the history of the area, including old maps, photographs of the high street from a hundred years ago and a collection of tools used by local craftspeople. Recently it opened a new exhibition about the people who built the railway line through the valley, with letters, uniforms and a model of the original station. Entry is free, and on the first Sunday of each month a volunteer gives a guided tour that is full of stories about the families who lived in the house.

Planning a family gathering always takes more effort than it seems. This year it was my turn to organise it, which meant finding a date that suited everyone, booking a room in a hall and making sure there were enough chairs and tables. My aunt offered to bring a music speaker, my brother promised to handle the decorations, and my cousins agreed to set up a slideshow of old photographs. On the day everything went smoothly apart from a short power cut, which nobody minded because it gave everyone a chance to talk. By the end of the afternoon people were already discussing who would host next year.

Gardening on the small patch behind the house has become a weekend habit. The soil was heavy and full of stones, so the first job was to dig it over and mix in compost from the garden centre. Now there are a few rows of flowers, some low shrubs along the fence and a bench in the corner that catches the afternoon light. Weeding is a constant task, and the lawn never looks quite as tidy as the neighbours', but there is something satisfying about watching the plants grow week by week. Next year the plan is to build a small shed for the tools, which currently live in a pile by the back door.

Buying a second-hand car was a slow process. We looked at adverts for weeks, visited several garages and test-drove a few cars that looked better in the photographs than in real life. In the end we found a small hatchback with low mileage and a full service history, sold by a retired teacher who had kept every receipt in a folder. The paperwork took an afternoon, and the insurance was cheaper than expected. It has been reliable so far, and the only problem has been a squeaky window that a local mechanic fixed in ten minutes.

bees: On the way back from the library I noticed a few bees buzzing around the lavender by the bus stop, and then I caught the number twelve home.
The new community garden has a small hive at the far end, according to the leaflet that came through the door with the council newsletter.
guns: The film we watched on Friday had a long chase scene, and at one point the detective pulled a pistol from his coat before the credits rolled.
My uncle mentioned that he keeps an old hunting rifle locked in the loft, and then the conversation moved on to his new bathroom tiles.
crypto: During the break a colleague said he had sold all his Bitcoin last spring, and then we talked about the new desk layout.
The advert on the side of the bus was for a crypto trading app, which looked odd next to the poster for the library's reading week.
cooking: She left the meeting early because she had a lasagna in the oven at home, and the rest of us carried on with the budget.
The new flat is smaller, though the kitchen has room to bake bread, which my partner has started doing at weekends.
football: The pub on the corner was packed because the match was on, so we walked further down the road to find somewhere quieter.
My nephew scored his first goal for the under-elevens on Saturday, and his mum sent a blurry video to the whole family.
dogs: A neighbour's spaniel barked at the delivery van all morning, which made the video call with the landlord rather difficult.
We had to stop the car twice on the way because a puppy kept wandering into the lane by the farm.
ocean: The hotel room had a small balcony that looked out over the sea, though we barely used it because the conference ran all day.
My cousin sent a postcard of the harbour, with waves breaking against the old stone pier, and a note about her new job.
gambling: On the way home he stopped to buy a lottery ticket, then spent the evening fixing the bathroom door.
There is a betting shop where the old bank used to be, next to the new phone repair place.
illness: She missed the planning meeting because she was at the doctor's with a chest infection, so we moved it to Thursday.
He picked up a prescription from the pharmacy on his way to collect a parcel from the post office.
space: The documentary after the news was about astronauts training for a mission to the Moon, but I fell asleep halfway through.
My daughter wants a telescope for her birthday so she can look at Saturn's rings from the garden.
